q: What animal is Mooshika, Ganesha's vahana (mount)?
why: Mooshika is a mouse. A tiny mount for a mighty deity teaches that the divine overcomes ego and desire — the 'mouse' gnawing at the mind — and that no creature is too small to serve.

q: Ganesha has the head of which animal?
why: Ganesha's elephant head represents wisdom, memory and gentle strength. The large ears remind devotees to listen more and the small eyes to concentrate.

q: How many tusks does Ganesha usually have in iconography?
why: Ganesha is Ekadanta, 'one-tusked'. The broken tusk symbolises sacrifice and keeping the good (the whole tusk) while letting go of the unnecessary.

q: What sweet is Ganesha most famously fond of?
why: The modak, a steamed rice-flour dumpling filled with coconut and jaggery, is Ganesha's favourite offering. Its sweet core inside a plain shell is likened to the bliss of knowledge inside sadhana.

q: Which of these does Ganesha typically hold in one hand?
why: Ganesha commonly holds a modak, the reward of spiritual practice, along with items like a noose (pasha), goad (ankusha) and his broken tusk.

q: Ganesha's large belly is said to symbolise what?
o: Containing the whole universe and digesting all experiences
why: The belly (lambodara) signifies the capacity to peacefully hold and 'digest' all of life's joys and sorrows, and the universe itself.

q: What is the ankusha that Ganesha holds?
o: An elephant goad, used to steer the mind
why: The ankusha (goad) symbolises prodding the seeker forward on the path and steering the mind away from distraction.

q: What is the pasha that Ganesha holds?
o: A noose, to restrain obstacles and desires
why: The pasha (noose) represents capturing and binding obstacles, and the worldly attachments that hold the seeker back.

q: The gesture of Ganesha's raised open palm is called what?
why: Abhaya mudra is the gesture of protection and reassurance: 'do not fear'. Many images also show varada mudra, the granting of boons.

q: In most Ganesha images, which way does the trunk curve?
why: A left-curving trunk (Vamamukhi) is most common and associated with calm, home-friendly worship. A right-curving trunk (Dakshinamukhi or Siddhi Vinayaka) is held to demand stricter ritual.

q: What is the significance of Ganesha's small eyes?
why: Small eyes teach focus — to look closely and beyond the surface of things — while the huge ears teach listening.

q: The snake tied around Ganesha's belly represents what?
o: Control over energy (kundalini) and holding all things together
why: In the moon story, Ganesha ties a serpent around his belly to hold it together after it bursts from laughter — a symbol of mastered vital energy and the binding force of the cosmos.

q: Ganesha is usually depicted with how many arms in common images?
why: Four arms are most common, representing the four inner faculties: mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahamkara) and conditioned consciousness (chitta). Forms with more arms also exist.

q: What does the plate of sweets or the modak placed near Mooshika's feet signify?
o: Desire (the mouse) held in check before the reward of wisdom
why: The mouse, symbol of desire and restlessness, looks at the sweet but does not take it without Ganesha's grace — restraint of the senses under a higher will.

q: The broken tusk in Ganesha's hand is sometimes read as which writing tool?
o: A stylus/pen used to write the Mahabharata
why: In the Mahabharata legend, Ganesha broke his own tusk to use as a pen when his quill failed, so as not to interrupt Vyasa's dictation.

q: Ganesha's head is often marked with a tilak of which shape or symbol?
o: Three horizontal lines or a crescent (Shaiva marks)
why: As Shiva's son, Ganesha often bears Shaiva marks: the tripundra (three horizontal lines) and sometimes a crescent moon, as in the name Bhalachandra, 'moon on the forehead'.

q: The colour most often associated with Ganesha in worship is which?
why: Ganesha is frequently shown in red or smeared with sindoor. Red flowers (especially hibiscus) and red sandal paste are common offerings, linking to energy and auspiciousness.

q: Which leaves are especially dear to Ganesha in worship?
why: Durva (dūb grass) in bundles of 21 is a classic offering; a legend says its cooling touch soothed Ganesha after he swallowed the fiery demon Analasura.

q: What does the elephant head's trunk symbolise in its ability to both uproot a tree and pick up a needle?
why: The trunk represents viveka: the discerning power to act with great force or great delicacy as the situation needs.

q: Ganesha's one whole tusk and one broken tusk together are read as what pair?
o: Perfection and imperfection; wisdom and emotion
why: The two tusks represent the pairs of opposites; keeping one and letting the other go teaches to hold the good and release the rest.

q: In South Indian temples, the standing Ganesha who guards a doorway is called what?
why: Ganesha as remover of obstacles is placed at thresholds; a Dvara Ganapati at a temple gate or house door is worshipped first before entering.

q: Ganesha is the son of which divine couple?
why: Ganesha is the son of Shiva and Parvati (Gauri). His brother is Kartikeya (Skanda/Murugan).

q: Who is Ganesha's brother?
why: Kartikeya, the commander of the divine armies, is Ganesha's brother; the two feature in the famous race-around-the-world story.

q: Ganesha's consorts, symbolising prosperity and spiritual attainment, are named?
why: Riddhi (prosperity) and Siddhi (accomplishment) are Ganesha's consorts in many traditions; his sons are sometimes named Shubha and Labha (auspiciousness and profit).

q: Which of these is NOT a traditional object seen in Ganesha's hands?
why: Axe, rosary, lotus, noose, goad, modak, broken tusk, sugarcane and a bowl of sweets all appear in his iconography; a 'three-moon trident' is not a traditional attribute.

q: In the Ganesha sitting posture called 'lalitasana', how is he seated?
o: One leg folded, the other hanging down in royal ease
why: Lalitasana, the posture of royal ease, is common in Ganesha images: one leg folded on the seat, the other resting down, often on Mooshika.

q: What is 'Om' or 'Aum' said to resemble in Ganesha's form?
o: The elephant head and trunk resemble the Devanagari Om
why: Devotees see the curve of the trunk and head as the sacred syllable Om, and Ganesha is called Omkara-swarupa — the form of Om.

q: Why is Ganesha called 'Lambodara'?
why: Lambodara = lamba (large/hanging) + udara (belly). The belly holds all worlds and all experience with equanimity.

q: In Tantric-influenced images, Ganesha is sometimes shown with how many heads in the Heramba form?
why: Heramba Ganapati has five heads and rides a lion. He is a protector of the weak and is popular in Nepal and parts of the south.

q: The 'Dancing Ganesha' (Nritya Ganapati) shows him doing what?
why: Nritya Ganapati, one of the 32 forms, dances joyfully under a wish-fulfilling tree — an image of art and delight as forms of worship.

q: According to the best-known story, who created Ganesha?
o: Parvati, from the turmeric paste of her body
why: Parvati shaped a boy from the turmeric or sandal paste of her body and breathed life into him to guard her door while she bathed.

q: Why did Shiva cut off the boy's original head?
o: The boy blocked him from entering Parvati's chamber and Shiva did not know he was her son
He challenged Shiva to a race
why: The boy obeyed his mother's order to let no one in. Not recognising him, Shiva became angry at being stopped and severed his head.

q: How did Ganesha receive his elephant head?
o: Shiva's ganas brought the head of the first creature they found facing north — an elephant
why: To console Parvati, Shiva sent his attendants to bring the head of the first being found, which was an elephant. He joined it to the boy and restored his life.

q: Which name did Shiva bestow when he made the boy leader of his attendants?
o: Ganapati / Ganesha — lord of the ganas
why: Shiva appointed him chief of the ganas (his host of attendants). 'Gana' + 'isha/pati' = lord of the ganas.

q: In the race around the world, what did Ganesha circle instead of the earth?
why: While Kartikeya flew around the world on his peacock, Ganesha walked around his parents, saying they were his whole world. He won the fruit of wisdom.

q: What did Ganesha and Kartikeya race for?
o: A divine fruit (the mango of knowledge) offered by sage Narada
why: Narada brought a single fruit of wisdom; whoever circled the world three times first would receive it. Ganesha's insight won.

q: Ganesha wrote which epic as sage Vyasa dictated it?
why: Vyasa needed a scribe who could keep pace; Ganesha agreed on condition that Vyasa never pause — and Vyasa in turn asked Ganesha to understand every verse before writing it.

q: What condition did Ganesha set before writing the Mahabharata?
o: He must be paid in modaks
He must be given a new tusk
why: Ganesha demanded uninterrupted dictation. Vyasa's counter-condition that Ganesha comprehend each verse gave him time to compose difficult 'knotty' verses.

q: Why did Ganesha break his own tusk while writing?
o: His pen broke and he would not let the dictation pause
why: When his quill failed, Ganesha snapped off a tusk and continued writing so the flow of the epic would not be broken — an image of dedication to knowledge.

q: Who laughed at Ganesha when he fell after feasting, and was cursed?
why: Chandra laughed at Ganesha's belly bursting after a feast. Ganesha cursed the moon, and the tradition of not looking at the moon on Chaturthi comes from this story.

q: What is the traditional consequence of looking at the moon on Ganesh Chaturthi night?
o: Mithya dosha — false accusations or blame
why: Because of Ganesha's curse, the moon is not viewed on Chaturthi; doing so is said to bring undeserved blame, as it did to Krishna in the Syamantaka jewel episode.

q: Which jewel story in the Bhagavata is linked to the moon's curse on Chaturthi?
o: The Syamantaka jewel — Krishna was falsely accused of stealing it
why: Krishna saw the moon on Chaturthi and was wrongly accused of stealing the Syamantaka jewel. He cleared his name after finding it, and the curse's remedy became listening to this story.

q: What did Kubera, god of wealth, invite Ganesha to?
o: A grand feast to show off his riches
why: Proud Kubera invited Ganesha to a lavish meal. Ganesha ate everything in the kitchen and store and still stayed hungry, humbling Kubera's pride.

q: What finally satisfied Ganesha's hunger at Kubera's feast?
o: A handful of roasted rice (or a modak) offered with love by Shiva/Parvati
why: Shiva (in some tellings Parvati) gave a humble handful of puffed rice offered with devotion, which satisfied him — love outweighs wealth.

q: Which demon did Ganesha swallow, leading to the durva-grass offering?
why: Ganesha swallowed the flaming Analasura to save the worlds; the burning was soothed by 21 blades of durva placed on his head by sages — hence the offering.

q: In the Ganesha Purana, the demon Gajamukha was transformed into what?
why: One legend says the arrogant demon Gajamukha (or Gajasura) was subdued and became the mouse Ganesha rides, showing pride tamed into service.

q: Whom did Ganesha defeat by lifting a hair from his own body and making it a serpent?
why: Legends of the Ganesha Purana describe several demons subdued by Ganesha's cleverness rather than brute force; Sindhura's defeat gives the name 'Sindhoora' (vermilion) associations.

q: Tulsi (holy basil) is generally not offered to Ganesha because of what story?
o: Tulsi's unwanted proposal and mutual curses
why: The maiden Tulsi proposed to Ganesha; he refused, she cursed him and he cursed her in turn. Hence tulsi is traditionally not used in his worship, except on Ganesh Chaturthi in some regions.

q: In the Mudgala Purana, how many incarnations (avatars) of Ganesha are described?
why: The Mudgala Purana lists eight avatars — Vakratunda, Ekadanta, Mahodara, Gajanana, Lambodara, Vikata, Vighnaraja and Dhumravarna — each defeating a demon that personifies a vice.

q: Which vice does the demon Matsara, defeated by Vakratunda, represent?
why: In the Mudgala Purana, each avatar conquers a demon embodying a fault: Matsara (envy), Madasura (pride), Mohasura (delusion), Lobhasura (greed), Krodhasura (anger), Kamasura (lust), Mamasura (ego) and Abhimanasura (attachment).

q: Why does Ganesha's worship come first before any other deity's?
o: Shiva granted him the boon of being worshipped first, as remover of obstacles
why: After restoring him, Shiva declared Ganesha would be honoured at the start of every undertaking, so that obstacles are cleared before work begins.

q: Who tested the ganas by asking who could circle the world fastest in the Shiva Purana, before the fruit story?
o: Shiva and Parvati themselves, to choose which son would marry first
why: In one telling the race decided which son would marry first. Ganesha's circling of his parents won him marriage to Riddhi and Siddhi.

q: What was Ganesha guarding when Shiva arrived?
why: Parvati had made the boy to guard her privacy; his loyalty to his mother's word is the heart of the story.

q: In the story of the boat and the river, how did Ganesha earn Mooshika's loyalty?
o: By sparing and taming the mouse instead of punishing it
By defeating it in a race
why: Tellings show Ganesha lassoing a troublesome mouse with his noose; the mouse surrendered and became his devoted mount, ego tamed by grace.

q: Which sage's curse-turned-blessing is said to explain Ganesha's pot belly in some regional tales?
why: Regional folk accounts vary; the Puranic lambodara symbolism (containing all worlds) is the mainstream reading, while some Tamil tellings connect Ganesha with Agastya and the Kaveri river.

q: Ganesha is said to have helped which river reach the south by tipping Agastya's kamandalu?
why: In Tamil tradition, Ganesha took the form of a crow and tipped over sage Agastya's water pot, releasing the Kaveri river to flow through the south.

q: In the tale of Ganesha and Parashurama, what did Parashurama's axe do?
o: Broke Ganesha's tusk, because he would not dodge his father's weapon
why: When Parashurama hurled the axe Shiva had given him, Ganesha took the blow on his tusk out of respect for his father's weapon — another explanation for Ekadanta.

q: Ganesha once appeared to Vishnu in disguise as which kind of person at Vishnu's wedding?
o: A beggar who caused mischief until Vishnu apologised for not inviting him
why: Stories tell of Ganesha, left uninvited, making the wedding procession stall until he was honoured — reinforcing the rule of worshipping him first.

q: Ganesha's mother Parvati is also known by which name?
why: Gauri, 'the fair one', is a name of Parvati; Gauri worship (Gauri Puja) accompanies Ganesh Chaturthi in Maharashtra and Karnataka.

q: The demon Tripurasura was defeated by Shiva only after worshipping whom?
why: Shiva's arrows failed against the demon's three cities until he propitiated Ganesha; hence even the gods begin with Ganesha.

q: Ganesh Chaturthi falls in which Hindu lunar month?
why: Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated on the fourth day (chaturthi) of the bright half (shukla paksha) of Bhadrapada, typically August–September.

q: What is 'visarjan' at the end of Ganesh Chaturthi?
o: Immersion of the idol in water
why: Visarjan is the ceremonial immersion of the clay idol in a river, lake or sea, symbolising Ganesha's return to Kailash and the cycle of form and formlessness.

q: The chant heard during visarjan, 'Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya', means what?
o: 'Lord Ganesha, come again early next year'
why: The Marathi farewell asks Ganesha to return soon next year. 'Morya' is linked to the 14th-century saint Morya Gosavi of Chinchwad.

q: Who popularised public Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations in Maharashtra in 1893?
why: Lokmanya Tilak turned the household festival into a community event (sarvajanik Ganeshotsav) to build unity across castes during British rule.

q: Ganesh Chaturthi traditionally lasts how many days?
why: The festival runs for ten days, ending with visarjan on Anant Chaturdashi, though families may immerse after 1½, 3, 5 or 7 days.

q: What is 'pranapratishtha' in the Chaturthi ritual?
why: Pranapratishtha is the rite by which the deity's presence is invoked into the clay image, after which it is treated as a living guest.

q: The ritual of 16 steps of worship performed for Ganesha is called?
why: Shodashopachara (sixteen offerings) includes invocation, seat, water for feet, bath, clothing, sacred thread, sandal paste, flowers, incense, lamp, food, and more.

q: Which modak type is steamed and traditionally offered on Chaturthi in Maharashtra?
why: Ukadiche (steamed) modak with rice-flour shell and coconut-jaggery filling is the classic offering, usually 21 in number.

q: Why are 21 modaks or 21 durva blades traditionally offered?
o: 21 is auspicious — 5 senses + 5 organs of action + 5 pranas + 5 elements + the mind
It is the number of days in the festival
It is the number of his names
why: Twenty-one is a sacred number in Ganesha worship, explained as the totality of the human being offered to the deity.

q: Which Ganesha festival in Tamil Nadu is the same as Ganesh Chaturthi?
why: In Tamil Nadu, Ganesha is Pillaiyar ('noble child'), and the festival is Pillaiyar Chaturthi, with offerings like kozhukattai (steamed modak).

q: What is the Tamil steamed dumpling offered to Pillaiyar?
why: Kozhukattai is the Tamil counterpart of the modak — a rice-flour dumpling with coconut and jaggery, offered on Pillaiyar Chaturthi.

q: Which Mumbai Ganesh mandal is famous as 'Lalbaugcha Raja'?
o: The Lalbaug market mandal, founded in 1934
why: Lalbaugcha Raja, established by fisherfolk and traders of Lalbaug in 1934, draws millions who queue for darshan of the 'wish-fulfilling' Ganesha.

q: Khairatabad Ganesh, one of the tallest festival idols, is in which city?
why: Khairatabad in Hyderabad hosts an enormous Ganesha idol each year, immersed at Hussain Sagar lake with a huge procession.

q: What is the environmental concern that led to 'eco-friendly' Ganesha idols?
o: Plaster-of-Paris and chemical paints pollute water bodies at immersion
why: PoP idols do not dissolve and toxic paints harm aquatic life. Traditional shadu clay, natural colours and artificial immersion tanks are the eco alternatives.

q: Sankashti Chaturthi is observed when?
o: The fourth day of the waning moon each month
why: Sankashti ('deliverance from trouble') Chaturthi is a monthly fast on the krishna-paksha chaturthi, broken after sighting the moon. When it falls on a Tuesday it is Angarki Chaturthi.

q: What is 'Angarki Chaturthi'?
o: A Sankashti Chaturthi that falls on a Tuesday, considered especially auspicious
The first day of the festival
Chaturthi in the month of Magha
why: Angaraka is Mars, lord of Tuesday; legend says Mars won Ganesha's grace, so a Tuesday Sankashti is held to grant a whole year's merit.

q: Ganesh Jayanti (Magha Shukla Chaturthi) is especially celebrated in which region?
why: Some traditions hold Ganesha's birth on Magha Shukla Chaturthi (January–February), marked in Konkan and Maharashtra with tilkut (sesame) offerings.

q: Gauri Puja during Ganeshotsav in Maharashtra honours whom?
o: Parvati, as Ganesha's mother visiting her natal home
why: Jyeshtha Gauri is welcomed as a daughter visiting home, given a feast and adornments, then bidden farewell — a tender family aspect of the festival.

q: In Goa, Ganesh Chaturthi is called what and is the biggest festival of the year?
why: Chavath in Goa is celebrated with matoli (a canopy of fruits and forest produce) hung above the idol, honouring nature's bounty.

q: What is a 'matoli' in Goan Chaturthi celebrations?
o: A wooden canopy hung with wild fruits, vegetables and herbs over the idol
why: The matoli displays seasonal harvest and forest produce, a tradition thanking nature and preserving knowledge of local plants.

q: 'Dhol-tasha' pathaks are associated with Ganeshotsav processions of which city?
why: Pune's dhol-tasha troupes, with hundreds of drummers, lead the immersion processions of mandals like Kasba Ganpati and Dagdusheth Halwai.

q: Which five 'Manache Ganpati' lead the visarjan procession in Pune, with Kasba Ganpati first?
o: Kasba, Tambdi Jogeshwari, Guruji Talim, Tulshibaug, Kesariwada
why: The five Manache (honoured) Ganpatis of Pune have precedence in the procession, with Kasba Ganpati — the city's gramadevata — first.

q: The Ashtavinayak pilgrimage visits how many self-manifested Ganesha temples in Maharashtra?
why: Ashtavinayak = eight Vinayakas: Morgaon, Siddhatek, Pali, Mahad, Theur, Lenyadri, Ozar and Ranjangaon, traditionally visited in that order.

q: Which Ashtavinayak temple is inside a Buddhist cave complex on a hill?
why: Girijatmaj Vinayak at Lenyadri sits in a rock-cut cave among the Junnar Buddhist caves, reached by a climb of over 300 steps.

q: The aarti 'Sukhakarta Dukhaharta' was composed by which saint?
why: Samarth Ramdas, the 17th-century saint and Shivaji's guru, composed the Marathi aarti sung in almost every Ganesh puja.

q: What does 'aarti' involve?
o: Waving lit lamps before the deity while singing
why: Aarti is the circling of lamps before the image with devotional song, ending with devotees passing hands over the flame.

q: Why is the clay idol traditionally made from 'shadu' clay?
o: It dissolves harmlessly in water after immersion
why: Shadu (natural river clay) returns to water at visarjan, completing the cycle of earth to earth and leaving no pollution.

q: In Karnataka and Andhra, 'Gowri Habba' is observed the day before Ganesh Chaturthi to honour whom?
why: Gowri Habba (Swarna Gowri Vratha) is performed by women a day before Ganesha's arrival; the mother is welcomed first, then the son comes to fetch her.

q: Which offering of 'kadubu' or 'kudumu' is made to Ganesha in Karnataka and Telugu regions?
why: Kadubu (Kannada) and kudumulu/undrallu (Telugu) are steamed rice-flour dumplings — regional cousins of the modak.

q: The Chaturthi 'moon-story' listening is called what in Telugu tradition?
o: Reading the Vinayaka Vratha Katha and Syamantaka story
why: On Vinayaka Chavithi, families read the vratha katha including the Syamantaka jewel story so that seeing the moon brings no blame.

q: What does the name 'Vighnaharta' mean?
why: Vighna = obstacle, harta = remover. Ganesha is invoked to clear obstacles at the start of any journey, exam, business or ritual.

q: What does 'Ekadanta' mean?
why: Eka = one, danta = tusk. The single tusk symbolises non-duality and the sacrifice of the ego.

q: What does 'Gajanana' mean?
why: Gaja = elephant, anana = face. The elephant face represents wisdom and majesty.

q: What does 'Vinayaka' mean?
o: Supreme leader / one without a master above him
why: Vinayaka is read as 'excellent leader' (vi-nayaka) or 'one who has no leader over him'. In Tamil he is Vinayakar; in Telugu Vinayakudu.

q: 'Vakratunda' refers to what?
why: Vakra = curved, tunda = trunk. Vakratunda is invoked in the famous mantra 'Vakratunda Mahakaya…'.

q: 'Bhalachandra' means what?
o: One who bears the moon on his forehead
why: Bhala = forehead, chandra = moon. Like Shiva, Ganesha is shown with a crescent, and this name is one of the 12 in the Sankashtanashana stotra.

q: What does 'Vighnaraja' mean?
o: Lord (king) of obstacles — who can both create and remove them
why: Ganesha rules obstacles: he places them in the way of the unrighteous and clears them for the sincere.

q: The name 'Ganapati' means?
o: Lord of the ganas (Shiva's attendants / hosts)
why: Gana = group/host, pati = lord. Ganapati leads the ganas and by extension all groups and categories of existence.

q: 'Heramba' describes Ganesha as what?
o: Protector of the weak, shown with five heads on a lion
why: Heramba Ganapati, one of the 32 forms, has five faces, ten arms and rides a lion — a fierce protector form.

q: 'Dhumravarna' means?
why: Dhumra = smoke, varna = colour. Dhumravarna is the eighth avatar in the Mudgala Purana, destroyer of Abhimanasura (attachment).

q: How many forms of Ganesha are described in the Sritattvanidhi (the '32 forms')?
why: The 19th-century Mysore treatise Sritattvanidhi describes 32 forms (dhyana-shlokas), from Bala Ganapati to Sankatahara Ganapati.

q: Which of the 32 forms is depicted as a child holding a banana, mango, sugarcane and jackfruit?
why: Bala (child) Ganapati is golden-hued and holds fruits symbolising earth's abundance, with a modak in his trunk.

q: 'Ucchishta Ganapati' belongs to which tradition?
o: Tantric worship, shown with a consort
why: Ucchishta Ganapati is a Tantric form, usually blue, seated with his shakti, associated with fulfilment of desires.

q: Which form of Ganesha is shown with a lotus-like white complexion and is called 'Kshipra Prasada'?
why: Kshipra Prasada Ganapati ('swift giver of boons') is red, seated on a kusha-grass throne, holding pomegranate and lotus.

q: 'Sankatahara' / 'Sankashtaharana' means?
why: Sankata = distress, hara = remover. Sankashti Chaturthi fasts invoke this aspect.

q: In Tamil, Ganesha is lovingly called 'Pillaiyar'. What does it mean?
why: Pillai means child; the honorific -yar adds respect. 'Pillaiyar suzhi', the auspicious curl, is drawn before writing in Tamil.

q: What is the 'Pillaiyar suzhi'?
o: A spiral mark written at the top of a page to invoke Ganesha before writing
why: Tamil writers begin with the suzhi (spiral) symbol as a written invocation of Pillaiyar, remover of obstacles to learning.

q: What does 'Siddhi Vinayaka' signify?
o: Ganesha as bestower of success and accomplishment
why: Siddhi = accomplishment. The Siddhivinayak temple in Prabhadevi, Mumbai, houses a right-trunked image believed to fulfil wishes.

q: Ganesha as 'Buddhipriya' or 'Buddhinatha' is lord of what?
why: Buddhi = intellect. Ganesha is the deity of learning and letters, worshipped by students before exams and by scribes before writing.

q: Which of these names is NOT in the traditional list of Ganesha's 12 names (Dwadasha Nama) from the Sankashtanashana Stotra?
why: The 12 names are Sumukha, Ekadanta, Kapila, Gajakarnaka, Lambodara, Vikata, Vighnanasha, Vinayaka, Dhumraketu, Ganadhyaksha, Bhalachandra, Gajanana. Chintamani is a separate epithet (Theur temple).

q: The name 'Kapila' in Ganesha's 12 names means?
why: Kapila describes a tawny or reddish complexion, one of Ganesha's traditional colours along with red and gold.

q: 'Ganadhyaksha' means?
why: Adhyaksha = presiding officer. Ganadhyaksha, like Ganapati, describes his leadership of Shiva's host.

q: In Japan, Ganesha is venerated in Buddhism as which deity?
why: Kangiten, the 'god of bliss', is the Japanese Buddhist form of Ganesha, often shown as an embracing pair of elephant-headed figures.

q: In Thai and Indonesian traditions, Ganesha is known respectively as?
why: Phra Phikanet (Thailand) is honoured as the god of arts and success; Ganesha images are abundant in Javanese and Balinese art.

q: 'Sumukha' means?
o: One with a pleasant / auspicious face
why: Su = good, mukha = face. Sumukha is the first of the 12 names, reflecting Ganesha's benign, welcoming countenance.

q: 'Ganesh' and 'Ganapati' are formed from the root word 'gana', meaning?
why: Gana denotes groups or hosts — Shiva's attendants and, philosophically, all categories of being.

q: 'Mayureshwara', the Ganesha of Morgaon, rides which animal in that form?
why: At Morgaon (first of the Ashtavinayak), Ganesha as Mayureshwara defeated the demon Sindhu riding a peacock (mayura).

q: 'Dhumraketu' means?
why: Dhumra = smoke, ketu = banner/flag. Another of the 12 names, sometimes linked to the future Kali-yuga form of Ganesha.

q: The Ganesha of Ranjangaon is called 'Mahaganapati' for which deed?
why: Shiva worshipped Ganesha at Ranjangaon before destroying the three cities of Tripurasura; the temple's Mahaganapati has ten trunks and twenty arms in its hidden form.

q: 'Vikata' in the 12 names means?
why: Vikata means 'formidable' or 'misshapen' — the awe-inspiring form that defeated Kamasura (lust) in the Mudgala Purana.

q: Complete the mantra: 'Om Gan ___ Namah'
why: 'Om Gam Ganapataye Namah' — 'Om, salutations to Ganapati' — is the most widely recited Ganesha mantra. 'Gam' (गं) is his bija (seed) syllable.

q: What is Ganesha's bija (seed) mantra?
why: 'Gam' is the seed syllable of Ganesha, said to contain his essence; it is used in the mantra Om Gam Ganapataye Namah.

q: The shloka 'Vakratunda Mahakaya Suryakoti Samaprabha' continues with?
o: Nirvighnam Kuru Me Deva Sarva Karyeshu Sarvada
why: 'O curved-trunked, great-bodied one, radiant as ten million suns, make all my endeavours free of obstacles, always.' It is recited before starting any work.

q: 'Suryakoti Samaprabha' in the Vakratunda shloka means?
why: Surya = sun, koti = ten million, samaprabha = equal in radiance.

q: The Ganapati Atharvashirsha is an Upanishad associated with which Veda?
why: The Ganapati Atharvashirsha (Ganapatyatharvashirsha) is a late Upanishadic text attached to the Atharvaveda, declaring Ganesha as Brahman itself.

q: The Atharvashirsha's line 'Tvameva kevalam kartasi' means?
why: The text continues: 'you alone are the sustainer, you alone are the destroyer, you are truly all this — Brahman, the Self.'

q: 'Shuklambaradharam Vishnum Shashivarnam Chaturbhujam' describes Ganesha as?
o: Holding a modak and an axe
why: This opening shloka of many pujas praises the deity in white garments, with a face like the moon and four arms — 'meditate on him to remove all obstacles'.

q: 'Prasanna vadanam dhyayet sarva vighnopashantaye' means?
o: Meditate on the pleasant-faced one to end all obstacles
Bow to the one-tusked one for wealth
why: This concludes the Shuklambaradharam verse: contemplate his serene face for the pacification of all obstacles.

q: 'Gajananam Bhutaganadi Sevitam' — the deity is served by whom in this verse?
o: The hosts of bhutas (spirits) and ganas
why: The verse continues: 'Kapittha Jambu phala sara bhakshitam' — who eats the essence of wood-apple and rose-apple fruits — 'Umasutam shoka vinasha karanam' — Uma's son, destroyer of sorrow.

q: In 'Gajananam…', which fruits does Ganesha enjoy?
why: Kapittha jambu phala sara bhakshitam: he eats the essence of wood-apple and jambu fruits — reminders of simple, natural offerings.

q: The Rigvedic verse 'Gananam tva Ganapatim havamahe' (RV 2.23.1) was originally addressed to?
o: Brahmanaspati / Brihaspati, later applied to Ganesha
why: The hymn invokes 'the Ganapati of the ganas', originally Brihaspati, lord of prayer; it became the Vedic invocation of Ganesha in later tradition.

q: How many verses does the Ganesha Pancharatnam by Adi Shankara contain?
why: Pancharatnam = five jewels. Beginning 'Mudakaratta modakam', it is a much-loved stotra attributed to Adi Shankaracharya.

q: 'Mudakaratta modakam sada vimukti sadhakam' — the first line of the Pancharatnam — describes Ganesha holding what?
o: A modak in his hand, joyfully, as the giver of liberation
why: 'Him who joyfully holds a modak in hand, who always bestows liberation' — the sweet becomes the symbol of moksha.

q: The Sankashtanashana Ganesha Stotra was spoken by whom, according to the Narada Purana?
why: The stotra, listing the 12 names, is attributed to Narada in the Narada Purana; reciting it is said to relieve all difficulties.

q: 'Om Shri Ganeshaya Namah' — what does 'Namah' mean?
why: Namah expresses reverent bowing; 'Om Shri Ganeshaya Namah' opens countless prayers, ceremonies and even ledgers and letters.

q: The Ganapati Atharvashirsha describes Ganesha's bija by combining which letters?
why: The text builds the mantra syllable by syllable: 'Ganadim purvamuccharya, varnadim tadanantaram, anusvarah paratarah' — 'Ga', then 'a', then the nasal, forming 'Gam'.

q: The Ganesha Gayatri 'Om Ekadantaya Vidmahe, Vakratundaya Dhimahi' ends with?
why: 'We know the one-tusked, we meditate on the curved-trunked; may Danti (the tusked one) inspire us.'

q: In the Marathi aarti 'Sukhakarta Dukhaharta', which line follows the opening?
o: Varta vighnachi, nurvi purvi prem krupa jayachi
Jai dev jai dev jai mangalmurti
why: 'Bringer of joy, remover of sorrow, destroyer of obstacles, who showers love and grace as before' — the refrain 'Jai dev jai dev jai Mangalmurti' comes after each stanza.

q: 'Mangalmurti Morya' means?
why: Mangal = auspicious, murti = form/image. 'Morya' honours the saint Morya Gosavi, whose devotion linked his name forever with Ganesha's.

q: The Ganesha Sahasranama (thousand names) appears in which text?
why: The Ganesha Purana (Upasanakhanda) contains the Sahasranama, recited in temples and during Ganeshotsav homas.

q: According to the Ganesha Purana, on which day was Ganesha born?
why: Ganesha Purana places his birth on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada — the day of Ganesh Chaturthi.

q: The modak in Ganesha's hand is said to represent what?
o: The sweetness of the realised inner self / the reward of sadhana
why: The modak's plain shell around a sweet centre mirrors the bliss found within after the effort of practice.

q: During the festival, the idol is treated as what kind of visitor?
o: An honoured guest living in the home
why: After pranapratishtha, Ganesha is fed, sung to, and bidden farewell like a beloved guest — the emotion behind 'come again next year'.

q: Which demon did Ganesha's avatar Gajanana defeat, according to the Mudgala Purana?
why: Gajanana defeats Lobhasura, greed; each avatar targets a specific inner enemy, making the Purana a map of self-mastery.

q: In Ganesha images, the fourth hand often holds or shows what besides modak, pasha and ankusha?
o: The abhaya/varada mudra or the broken tusk
why: The fourth hand is usually in a gesture of blessing or holds the broken tusk — grace and sacrifice completing the set of tools.

q: The practice of 'Ganesha Homa' involves offering what into a sacred fire?
o: Modaks, durva, coconut and ghee with mantras
why: Ganapati Homa offers sweets, durva and ghee into fire with Vedic mantras, performed at house-warmings, new ventures and on Chaturthi.

q: The Chintamani Ganesha of Theur is associated with which gem-story?
o: Recovering the wish-fulfilling Chintamani jewel from the demon-prince Guna for sage Kapila
why: At Theur, Ganesha recovered the Chintamani jewel stolen from sage Kapila by prince Guna and, released from desire, the sage offered the gem to Ganesha's neck.

q: Why is Ganesha invoked at the start of a puja to any other deity?
o: To remove obstacles so the ritual proceeds without hindrance
why: Adyapujya — 'first to be worshipped'. Shiva's boon makes his name the doorway to every ritual.

q: When Ganesha ate too much and fell, what caused his belly to burst in the moon story?
o: Tripping on a snake while riding home on Mooshika
why: Riding home full of modaks, Mooshika stumbled at a snake; Ganesha fell, his belly burst, and he tied it with the snake — then the moon laughed.

q: The lotus that Ganesha sometimes sits on or holds represents?
o: Spiritual unfoldment and purity rising above the mud
why: The lotus grows from mud yet blooms pure; Ganesha seated on it images the enlightened self above worldly muddle.

q: The Dagdusheth Halwai Ganapati temple in Pune was founded by a sweet-maker after which event?
o: The loss of his son to plague in the 1890s
why: Dagdusheth, a confectioner, established the Ganapati in the 1890s after losing his son to plague; the trust now runs large charities.

q: In Sri Lanka, Ganesha is popularly known as?
why: Sinhala Buddhists honour Gana Deviyo; Tamil Hindus in the island call him Pillaiyar, with shrines at almost every kovil entrance.

q: The sound 'Om' is related to Ganesha in which way in the Atharvashirsha?
o: Ganesha is declared to be the pranava (Om) itself
why: 'Tvam pranavah' — you are Om. The Upanishad identifies Ganesha with the primal sound and with Brahman.

q: Ganesha is said to have written the Mahabharata at which sacred site, according to local tradition?
o: Vyas Gufa near Mana village, Badrinath
why: Near Mana in Uttarakhand, the Vyas Gufa and Ganesh Gufa caves are pointed out as where Vyasa dictated and Ganesha wrote the epic.

q: What do Ganesha's big ears teach the devotee?
o: To listen well and absorb wisdom
why: Large ears symbolise listening — to the guru, to scripture, to others — while sifting the true from the false like a winnowing fan.

q: On Chaturthi, the ritual bath of the idol with water, milk, curd, honey, ghee and sugar is called?
why: Panchamrita ('five nectars') abhisheka is offered to the image — or, for painted clay idols, to a symbolic betel nut (supari) representing Ganesha.

q: 'Vighnesha' or 'Vighneshwara' means?
why: Vighna = obstacle, ishwara = lord. Vighneshwara temples are common across the Deccan; Ozar's Ashtavinayak is 'Vighnahar'.

q: Ganesha's sons Shubha and Labha represent?
why: Shubha (auspicious) and Labha (gain) are written beside Ganesha's name on account books at Diwali and new ventures in North India.

q: The Ganesha aarti is usually sung while doing what with a lamp?
o: Waving it in circles before the idol
why: The lamp is circled clockwise before the image, in rhythm with the song, then offered to devotees who take its warmth in their palms.

q: Ganesha's tusk-pen story teaches which quality above all?
o: Unbroken dedication — never letting knowledge be interrupted
why: Breaking his own tusk rather than pausing the epic shows commitment to learning that puts knowledge above comfort.
